questions.text:
Read this sentence:

'The classroom buzzed with nervous energy as students shuffled papers and exchanged worried glances.'

Which choice BEST identifies the mood AND explains how the language creates it?
options: Excited and joyful — created by the verb 'buzzed' which suggests happy energy
Anxious and tense — created by the cluster of negative words ('nervous', 'shuffled', 'worried glances') and the unsettled verb 'buzzed' which links to nervous, restless energy
Bored and tired — created by the slow movement of the students
Angry and aggressive — created by the silence in the room
questions.expectedAnswer: Anxious and tense — created by the cluster of negative words ('nervous', 'shuffled', 'worried glances') and the unsettled verb 'buzzed' which links to nervous, restless energy
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer identifies anxiety and explains HOW the words create it.

Here's why:
'Buzzed' on its own could be excited, but the surrounding words ('nervous', 'worried', 'shuffled') tell the reader the energy is anxious not joyful — context is everything.
Merit-level reading requires you to track multiple words together, not just one.
Exam tip: ask 'why has the writer chosen these particular verbs and adjectives together?'

questions.text:
'Her words cut through the silence like a knife.'

Identify the language feature used AND explain its effect on how the reader pictures her words.
options: Metaphor — her words are literally a knife
Simile — the comparison ('like a knife') makes her words feel sharp, sudden and even painful, suggesting they are harsh and impossible to ignore
Onomatopoeia — the word 'cut' imitates a sound
Hyperbole — her words actually broke the silence in half
questions.expectedAnswer: Simile — the comparison ('like a knife') makes her words feel sharp, sudden and even painful, suggesting they are harsh and impossible to ignore
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the simile option WITH the effect explanation.

Here's why:
The word 'like' makes this a SIMILE (a metaphor would be 'her words were a knife').
The knife comparison makes the reader feel the words are sharp, decisive and possibly hurtful.
Exam tip: be precise about simile vs metaphor — 'like' or 'as' = simile.

questions.text:
Read this passage:

'Grandad's workshop smelled of sawdust and stories. Every shelf held a memory — the wooden boat he carved for Mum, the chess set with the missing knight, the half-finished picture frame that would never be completed now.'

What can the reader INFER about Grandad and his relationship with the family from this short passage? Use TWO specific quotations from the text and explain what each one suggests.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per inference IF the answer includes a quote AND explains what it implies (not just what it literally says). 2 inferences required.

Examples of strong answers:

'the wooden boat he carved for Mum' — implies he was a skilled craftsman who made things by hand for the people he loved; he had a close relationship with the speaker's mother.

'the half-finished picture frame that would never be completed now' — the words 'never... now' imply that Grandad has died; this is a piece of evidence the reader has to put together themselves rather than being told directly.

'Every shelf held a memory' — the workshop functions as a kind of memorial; objects in it are valuable not for what they are but for what they represent.

'sawdust and stories' — pairs the physical (sawdust) with the abstract (stories), implying Grandad was both a maker AND a teller of tales who shaped the family's identity.

Do not award the second mark for vague answers without quotation.

questions.text: In the passage above, the phrase 'smelled of sawdust and stories' uses TWO language features at once. Identify them BOTH and briefly explain how 'stories' is being used in a non-literal way.
options: Alliteration ('sawdust and stories') AND metaphor — 'stories' do not literally have a smell, so the writer is suggesting the workshop is so full of memories and tales that they feel like part of the air
questions.expectedAnswer: Alliteration ('sawdust and stories') AND metaphor — 'stories' do not literally have a smell, so the writer is suggesting the workshop is so full of memories and tales that they feel like part of the air
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer identifies BOTH features and explains the metaphor.

Here's why:
Alliteration: the repeated 's' sound in 'sawdust and stories' creates rhythm and links the two ideas together.
Metaphor: 'stories' don't actually smell — the writer is implying that the workshop is so full of memories that they feel almost physical.
Exam tip: be ready for sentences that use TWO features at once — quote the same words for each feature.

questions.text:
Read this advertisement text:

'Tired of soggy sandwiches? Sick of the same old lunch? Revolution Wraps are here to rescue your taste buds! Made with 100% natural ingredients and wrapped in our signature whole-grain tortilla, you'll never look at lunch the same way again.'

Identify TWO different persuasive techniques used. For each one, quote the exact words AND explain how it tries to persuade the reader.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per technique IF the answer names the technique, quotes the words, AND explains the persuasive effect. 2 techniques required.

Examples of strong answers:

Rhetorical questions — 'Tired of soggy sandwiches? Sick of the same old lunch?' Effect: the questions assume the reader has a problem that needs solving, making them mentally agree before the product is even mentioned, and creating a feeling of being understood.

Personification / emotive language — 'rescue your taste buds!' Effect: by giving the wraps the heroic role of 'rescuer', the ad makes a simple lunch product feel exciting and life-changing.

Alliteration — 'soggy sandwiches'. Effect: makes the boring lunch sound especially unpleasant, while being catchy and memorable.

Fact / statistic — '100% natural ingredients'. Effect: targets health-conscious buyers and makes the product sound trustworthy by giving it a precise figure.

Hyperbole — 'never look at lunch the same way again'. Effect: deliberate exaggeration creates excitement and suggests the product is genuinely transformative.

Do NOT award the second mark for naming techniques without quotation and effect.

options: Tone is the writer's ATTITUDE towards their subject (e.g. sarcastic, admiring), while mood is the FEELING or atmosphere the text creates for the reader (e.g. tense, peaceful)
Tone and mood mean the same thing
Tone is the topic of the text, mood is the genre
Tone is the volume of the words on the page, mood is how loud they sound
questions.expectedAnswer: Tone is the writer's ATTITUDE towards their subject (e.g. sarcastic, admiring), while mood is the FEELING or atmosphere the text creates for the reader (e.g. tense, peaceful)
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer distinguishes tone (writer) from mood (reader).

Here's why:
Tone = the writer's attitude. Mood = how the text makes the reader feel.
A writer can use a humorous TONE (their attitude) to create a lighthearted MOOD (reader's feeling).
Exam tip: a useful test — if you can finish the sentence 'the writer feels...' you have identified the TONE; if you can finish 'this passage makes me feel...' you have identified the MOOD.

questions.text: A piece of writing about climate change has a sarcastic tone but creates an angry mood. Explain how this is possible — that is, how the WRITER's attitude (tone) and the READER's feeling (mood) can be different. Use a brief made-up example to illustrate your answer.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for clearly distinguishing tone (writer's attitude) and mood (reader's feeling), and explaining that they don't have to match.

1 mark for a clear, brief example that shows how a sarcastic tone might trigger anger in the reader.

Example of a strong answer: 'Tone is the writer's attitude — sarcasm shows the writer thinks something is ridiculous or wrong. Mood is the feeling the reader is left with. A writer who says "Oh sure, let's keep burning oil — what could possibly go wrong?" sounds amused or sarcastic (tone), but because the topic is serious, the reader actually feels angry that politicians are not acting (mood). The two work together: the sarcasm makes the reader uncomfortable enough to feel angry.'

Do NOT award full marks if the student confuses tone and mood, or gives no example.

questions.text:
Read this poem extract:

'The Waiting Room

Plastic chairs in rows like soldiers,
the clock's tick marking time
like a heartbeat slowing down.
A child builds towers from magazines
while her mother stares at the door —
that door which swallows people whole
and sometimes spits them back
changed.

We sit in the fluorescent glow,
strangers sharing the same silence,
the same prayers we won't say aloud.'

In an extended response, analyse how the poet creates a sense of TENSION and SHARED HUMAN EXPERIENCE. Your answer MUST cover ALL of the following:
• TWO specific language features (e.g. simile, metaphor, contrast) with quotations
• how the contrast between the CHILD and the ADULTS adds to the meaning
• how the FINAL STANZA brings the strangers together
• ONE inference about the SETTING that the reader has to work out from clues in the poem.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks total — award one for each bullet covered well.

1 mark — TWO language features with quotes:

Simile — 'Plastic chairs in rows like soldiers' (rigid, regimented, waiting for orders, cold and impersonal).

Simile — 'clock's tick... like a heartbeat slowing down' (time is dragging, but also linked to mortality).

Metaphor — 'that door which swallows people whole / and sometimes spits them back / changed' (the door as a hungry creature; the people who come out are altered).

1 mark — Contrast between the child and adults: the child innocently 'builds towers from magazines', unaware of what is happening; the adults, including her own mother, stare at the door consumed by worry. The contrast highlights how anxiety is something adults carry that the child cannot yet understand — and underlines the helplessness of waiting.

1 mark — Final stanza brings strangers together: 'strangers sharing the same silence, / the same prayers we won't say aloud' — the repetition of 'the same' and the shift from 'I' to 'we' creates a sense of unspoken solidarity. People who don't know each other are united by their common fear and hope.

1 mark — Inference about setting: clues such as 'fluorescent glow', 'plastic chairs', 'door which swallows people whole', and the prayers strongly imply this is a hospital waiting room — perhaps outside an operating theatre or intensive care unit. The poem never says 'hospital' but the reader works it out from the imagery.

Excellence-level answers will weave the bullets into one paragraph, not list them separately.
